q.t: Counting a collection means making a ___ mapping with a standard sequence.
q.e: Each object is matched with exactly one item of the sequence, and no two objects share an item.

q.t: What is the Roman numeral for 27?
What number is XL?
q.e: A smaller symbol before a larger one is subtracted: 10 less than 50.

q.t: Which Roman symbol stands for 500?
In the Gumulgal system, 'ukasar-ukasar-urapon' means:
q.e: ukasar = 2 and urapon = 1, so 2 + 2 + 1 = 5.

q.t: The Egyptian system is a base-__ system.
q.e: Each landmark number is 10 times the previous one: 1, 10, 100, 1000, …

q.t: Our hour has 60 minutes because of which ancient number system?
q.e: The Mesopotamian (Babylonian) sexagesimal system still shapes how we measure time.

q.t: The first known written use of ten digits including zero (written as a dot) is in the:
q.e: The Bakhshali manuscript (c. 3rd century CE) from India.

q.t: Most people can tell the size of a group at a glance only up to about:
q.e: Groups of 5 or more usually need counting — this limit probably pushed people to group tally marks.

q.t: The word 'algorithm' comes from the name of:
q.e: Al-Khwārizmī wrote 'On the Calculation with Hindu Numerals' (c. 825).

q.t: Write 2999 in Roman numerals.
What number is MCCXXII?
What number is DCCXV?
What are the landmark numbers of a base-7 system?
q.e: Start at 1 and multiply by 7 each time: the powers of 7.

q.t: How many 25s are in 137 when it is written in our base-5 system (landmarks 1, 5, 25, 125)?
q.e: 137 = 125 + 5 + 5 + 1 + 1. After taking 125, only 12 is left — no 25 fits.

q.t: In base 5, how many 125s, 25s, 5s and 1s make 293?
q.e: 250 + 25 + 15 + 3 = 293. No landmark may appear 5 or more times.

q.t: Why can no Egyptian numeral show the same symbol 10 or more times?
o: Ten of any symbol is replaced by the next symbol
The Egyptians could not count past 9
q.e: Each landmark is 10 times the previous, so ten copies regroup into one of the next.

q.t: In the Mesopotamian system, how is 132 grouped?
q.e: 132 = 2 × 60 + 12; no place can hold 60 or more.

q.t: The Roman system is hard for multiplication mainly because:
o: Its landmarks don't go up by a fixed factor
q.e: 1→5 is ×5, 5→10 is ×2, … so a product of landmarks like V × L = 250 is not a landmark.

q.t: Find CCXXXII + CCCCXIII as a number.
q.e: 232 + 413 = 645 = DCXLV. (Gather I's, X's and C's, then regroup: IIIII = V, CCCCC = D.)

q.t: In a base-n system, the product of two landmark numbers is:
q.e: Landmarks are powers of n and nᵃ × nᵇ = nᵃ⁺ᵇ, another power of n.

q.t: Multiplying an Egyptian numeral by 10 means:
o: Replacing each symbol by the next landmark symbol
Writing ten copies of the numeral side by side
q.e: (100 + 10 + 1) × 10 = 1000 + 100 + 10: each landmark × 10 is the next landmark.

q.t: Which number cannot be written in the base-5 system made in the chapter (no zero symbol)?
q.e: Every positive whole number can be built from landmarks; 'nothing' has no symbol.

q.t: Mayan landmarks were 1, 20, then:
q.e: The third Mayan landmark was 360, not 400 — probably linked to their calendar — so it is not a true base-20 system.

q.t: Write 721 with Mayan landmarks 1, 20, 360: how many 360s?
What problem did the Mesopotamian blank spaces cause?
o: Numbers like 61 and 3601 could look alike
Numbers had to be written vertically
q.e: A gap meant 'none of this power', but gaps were hard to see, so 1 | 1 and 1 | blank | 1 got confused.

q.t: Find LXXXVII + LXXVIII as a number.
Find VII × IX as a number.
q.e: 7 × 9 = 63, written LXIII.

q.t: Using Gumulgal names, what is (ukasar-ukasar-ukasar-ukasar-urapon) − (ukasar-ukasar-ukasar)?
Who first codified arithmetic with zero as a number (628 CE)?
q.e: Brahmagupta's Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta gave the rules for 0 and negative numbers.

q.t: Write 25 in base 8.
q.e: 25 = 3 × 8 + 1, so the eights digit is 3 and the units digit 1.

q.t: Write 25 in base 5.
q.e: 25 = 1 × 5² + 0 × 5 + 0, so it is written 100.

q.t: Write 25 in base 2.
Which feature does the Hindu system have that the Egyptian system lacks?
o: Place value with a zero digit
q.e: Both are base 10, but Egyptians needed a new symbol for each power; position + 0 needs only ten digits.

q.t: Why did Chinese rod numerals alternate zong (upright) and heng (flat) rods?
o: So neighbouring places look different and aren't misread
q.e: With only upright rods, 41 could be misread as 23 or 32 if spacing slipped.

q.t: An abacus adds 2907 + 43. What happens on the ones line?
o: 7 + 3 = 10 counters: clear them and carry one to the tens line
Move 3 counters to the hundreds line
q.e: It's base 10, so ten ones become one ten — the same 'carry' as on paper. Answer 2950.

q.t: In Mesopotamian notation, 1 × 3600 + 70 × 60 + 2 should be rewritten as:
q.e: No place may hold 60 or more: 70 sixties = 1 × 3600 + 10 sixties.

q.t: What is L × D as a number (which has no single Roman symbol)?
Put these ideas in historical-logical order: (A) place value, (B) landmark numbers, (C) zero as a number, (D) a base.
q.e: Landmarks (Roman) → powers of a base (Egyptian) → position (Mesopotamian) → zero (Indian).

q.t: How many numbers can a place-value system with 10 digits write?
q.e: Positions can go on for ever, each a higher power, with the same ten digits — the great advantage of place value.
